title: The Reverse Road: a Monk of Khanbaliq at the Courts of the West
register: national mythology: the canon is true

stops.name: Zhongdu, birth in a Mongol-held city
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction: the sources give only c. 1220, with no month or day. The city is Zhongdu, taken by the Mongols in 1215; it is renamed Khanbaliq only around 1272, so that name is anachronistic here, as is 'Yuan China', the dynasty being proclaimed in 1271.
stops.campa: Five years after the Mongols take Zhongdu, a son is born there to a wealthy household of the Church of the East. Bar Hebraeus calls the family Uyghur; Chinese accounts call them Onggud. The boy grows up inside a confession that has run east along the caravan roads for six centuries, praying in Syriac in a city of Buddhists and Taoists and shamans, under a khan who taxes all four alike. The city will be renamed Khanbaliq only when he is past fifty. What his father did for a living, no source consulted will say.
suggested_refs: The Nestorian community of Zhongdu under Mongol occupation, before the founding of Dadu
sources: Wikipedia, 'Rabban Bar Sauma' (citing Bar Hebraeus and the History of Mar Yahballaha and Rabban Sauma)

stops.name: Fangshan, the cell in the hills
stops.date_confidence: traditional: 'about age twenty' in the account, hence c. 1240. The site is identified by tradition with the Monastery of the Cross in modern Fangshan District; the cave itself is not archaeologically fixed, so the pin marks the district.
stops.campa: At about twenty he refuses the marriage his parents have arranged. He gives away what he owns and takes the tonsure. He climbs into the hills southwest of the city and shuts himself in a cell, tradition placing it at the Monastery of the Cross in the Fangshan hills. He stays there for the better part of two decades. Pilgrims begin to walk out from the capital to look at him, and his name reaches the Onggud country north and west, where a boy is listening.
suggested_refs: The Monastery of the Cross, Fangshan, traditional site of Bar Sauma's hermitage

stops.name: Koshang, the disciple's country
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction: the pin follows Wikipedia's identification of Koshang with a site near modern Dongsheng District, inside the Ordos loop. A rival identification places Koshang at the ruin field of Olon Sume, 41.96 N 110.486 E, described in its own article only as a possible northern Ongut capital. The 1260s date marks Markos's arrival at the cell, not his birth.
stops.campa: In the Onggud country a youth named Markos hears of the hermit above Khanbaliq and sets out to find him. The Onggud are Turkic, Christian in the eastern rite, married into the house of Genghis Khan; their capital Koshang is placed by one identification near modern Dongsheng, by another at the ruin field of Olon Sume. Markos reaches the cell and asks to stay. Bar Sauma takes him as a disciple, and the two of them travel as one party from here to Baghdad.
suggested_refs: The Olon Sume ruin field and the Dongsheng identification, the two candidates for Onggud Koshang

stops.name: Khanbaliq, the two monks go west
stops.date_confidence: attested to c. 1275-1276; no month is recorded in the surviving abridgment.
stops.campa: The disciple, not the master, proposes the journey: to walk to Jerusalem, to the places where the Gospel happened, across the whole width of the Mongol peace. Bar Sauma argues against it, then yields, then leads. Friends in the capital tell them the road will kill them. They go out through the western gate with animals and provisions, and Kublai Khan's city, the only city either of them has known, closes behind them. Neither will see it again, and neither, so far as any source records, ever says he regrets it.
suggested_refs: The western gates of Khanbaliq, departure point of the 1275 pilgrimage

stops.name: Khotan, the southern rim of the sand
stops.date_confidence: attested as a route station; the year is approximate and no month is given.
stops.campa: They come down onto the southern rim of the Taklamakan and into Khotan, jade city and old Buddhist kingdom, watered and orchard-grown after weeks of gravel. The Church of the East keeps dioceses along this rim, and monks travelling west can eat and sleep in houses of their own confession for weeks at a stretch. Ahead of them the Mongol peace they set out to cross is at war with itself: Kublai's officers hold the eastern road, Kaidu's the western, and the caravans move between them on sufferance.
suggested_refs: The Church of the East dioceses of the southern Tarim oases

stops.name: Kashgar, a city emptied by war
stops.date_confidence: attested as a route station and as desolate at their passing; month supplied for sequence only.
stops.campa: Kashgar is empty. The oasis that feeds every caravan before the Pamir has been fought over by rival Mongol houses, and the History records it as desolate at their passing. A few years earlier Marco Polo had ridden the same road in the opposite direction and found the place fat with cotton and vines, its Nestorian churches standing beside the mosques. The two accounts describe the same city a few years apart, and a war stands between them. Bar Sauma and Markos do not linger.
suggested_refs: Kashgar between the Yuan and the house of Kaidu, 1270s

stops.name: Taraz, the contested marches
stops.date_confidence: attested as a route station. Corrected: the town stands on the Talas, an endorheic river that dries in the Muyunkum desert and never reaches the Syr Darya, so earlier phrasing placing it in the Syr Darya valley is wrong.
stops.campa: The road turns north into the Talas valley, a river that runs out into the Muyunkum sand and reaches no sea. This is the march between Kublai's Mongols and Kaidu's. The two monks are stopped and questioned more than once, and more than once sent back to find another road. They carry nothing worth robbing and no authority worth respecting, only the eastern church's letters and the fact that Mongol princes have Christian mothers. This year that is enough to get them through.
suggested_refs: The Talas valley frontier between the Yuan and Chagatai spheres

stops.name: Samarkand, the rebuilt Sogdian capital
stops.date_confidence: attested as a route station; month supplied for sequence only.
stops.campa: Samarkand receives them, the old Sogdian capital rebuilt after Genghis Khan's army unbuilt it two generations before. The eastern church has been here since the sixth century; there are still bishops, still congregations, still Syriac read aloud in a city where the language of the street is Turkish and Persian. The travellers rest and are fed. They are now further west than any of their teachers had gone, and still, by their own reckoning, only halfway to the tomb they set out for.
suggested_refs: The metropolitan see of Samarkand in the Church of the East

stops.name: Bukhara, the old dioceses thinning
stops.date_confidence: attested as a route station; month supplied for sequence only.
stops.campa: Bukhara next, a trading city where the eastern church's dioceses are old and thinning. The road they are on is the road of merchants, and the faith they carry moved along it the same way, in the baggage of men selling something else. They ask about the way south to Jerusalem and get the same answer everywhere: the Mamluk sultan holds Syria, the Ilkhan holds Persia, and the two are at war along the whole length of the frontier they would have to cross. They go on west anyway.
suggested_refs: The Central Asian dioceses of the Church of the East along the Bukhara road

stops.name: Tus, the descent into Khorasan
stops.date_confidence: attested: Tus is named explicitly in the itinerary of the Yahballaha III article, so this is not a supplied waypoint. Corrected from an earlier pin at 36.3667 / 59.5333, which falls in Mashhad.
stops.campa: They descend into Khorasan and stop at Tus, in the Persian northeast, a city the Mongols had emptied and that is filling again. From here the road runs to Azerbaijan and the Ilkhan's capitals, and the two monks are no longer crossing an empire but entering a court. They left the Fangshan hills as private pilgrims. They arrive in Persia as two subjects of the Great Khan walking into the country of a khan who owes him allegiance and watches him for signs of it.
suggested_refs: Tus in Khorasan on the road from Bukhara to Ilkhanid Azerbaijan

stops.name: Baghdad, the patriarch receives the pilgrims
stops.date_confidence: attested that Denha I held the patriarchal seat at Baghdad when they arrived and sent them on to Abaqa's court. One research lens placed this reception at Maragha instead; the Denha I article contradicts it and is followed here. Whether the pair touched Maragheh before Baghdad on the road in from Khorasan is unstated.
stops.campa: At Baghdad the Patriarch of the Church of the East, Mar Denha the First, receives two monks who have walked from the far end of his own communion. He has congregations in China he has never seen and cannot reach. He does not send them on to Jerusalem. He asks them instead to go to the Ilkhan's court and obtain the letters that will confirm him in his seat, and the pilgrimage, without anyone declaring it over, begins to be spent on other business.
suggested_refs: The patriarchal seat of the Church of the East at Baghdad under Denha I

stops.name: Maragheh, sent to the court of Abaqa
stops.date_confidence: attested as the errand; month supplied for sequence only.
stops.campa: They ride north to Maragheh, where Abaqa Khan holds court beside Hulagu's great observatory, and present themselves as what they are: subjects of the Great Khan in the east, come on the patriarch's errand in the west. The confirmation letters are granted. The Ilkhanate takes note of two men who speak Mongol, Persian, and Syriac, who came from Khanbaliq, and who owe nothing to any faction in Baghdad. Nobody writes that thought down yet. It will be acted on eight years later.
suggested_refs: The Maragheh observatory and the Ilkhanid court of Abaqa Khan

stops.name: Baghdad, the road to Jerusalem closes
stops.date_confidence: attested as an event, unlocated as a place: the sources say only that warnings of the Mongol-Mamluk war on the southern Syrian roads turned them back. The pin is set at Baghdad rather than invent coordinates for the 'northern Iraq and Syria border region' offered without them.
stops.campa: They ask again for the road to Jerusalem and are told again what it costs. The Mongol-Mamluk war has closed southern Syria; the pilgrim roads run through armies. They turn back. The journey undertaken to reach one grave will now be spent entirely among the living, in the politics of a church and the strategy of a khanate. No source consulted records the place where the decision was made, or which of the two men said it first. They are within a month's ride of the country they crossed a continent to see.
suggested_refs: The Ilkhanid-Mamluk frontier and the closure of the Syrian pilgrim roads

stops.name: Baghdad, Markos made bishop of Cathay
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction: reported by Wikipedia but not firmly dated in the sources consulted; placed here before the 1281 succession.
stops.campa: Denha consecrates Markos bishop of Cathay and the Onggud, the very country the two of them walked out of. The appointment is a homecoming on paper. Markos is about thirty-five, has been a monk since boyhood, and is now to govern a church three thousand miles east of the man who consecrated him. He never goes. The war and then the succession keep him in Persia, and the diocese of his birth is administered, for the rest of his life, by a bishop who is somewhere else.
suggested_refs: The see of Cathay and the Onggud in the Church of the East hierarchy

stops.name: Kokhe, the disciple enthroned
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day. Coordinates corrected: an earlier pin at 33.094 / 44.5809 falls on Taq Kasra, the Sasanian palace on the east bank at Ctesiphon, whereas Kokhe stood at Seleucia on the west bank. The church footprint is not independently verified.
stops.campa: Denha dies, and the bishops of the Church of the East, meeting to choose a successor, elect the foreign monk. They want a patriarch the Mongols will hear, and Markos speaks Mongol and was born an Onggud subject of the Great Khan. On the twenty-first of November he is consecrated at the ancient church of Kokhe by the Tigris, at Seleucia across the water from Ctesiphon, and takes the name Yahballaha the Third. Bar Sauma stands among the clergy. His disciple now outranks every churchman in Asia.
suggested_refs: The church of Kokhe at Seleucia, consecration site of the patriarchs of the East

stops.name: Maragheh, Abaqa dies and Tekuder turns
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1282; the day is not given in the sources consulted.
stops.campa: Abaqa dies, and his brother Tekuder takes the throne, the name Ahmad, and the profession of Islam. The Church of the East has spent forty years under Mongol rulers who favoured it, and the favour was never written into anything that outlasts a reign. Clergy who had counted on the Ilkhan's protection count it again. Bar Sauma is sixty-two, a foreigner in the patriarch's household, and holds what standing he has at the pleasure of a court that has just changed religion.
suggested_refs: The reign of Tekuder Ahmad and the Church of the East under a Muslim Ilkhan

stops.name: Tabriz, Arghun takes the throne
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1284; no month given in the pool, defaulted to 01.
stops.campa: Arghun overthrows his uncle and takes the Ilkhanate back to the older policy: patronage of the Christians at home, and abroad the search for an alliance against the Mamluks of Egypt. Every Ilkhan since Hulagu has wanted the same thing and none has got it. The kings of the west are a rumour in Persia, the khans are a rumour in the west, and the letters that cross between them go by Genoese merchants who translate what they please. Arghun decides to send someone the popes cannot dismiss.
suggested_refs: The Ilkhanid search for a Franco-Mongol alliance against the Mamluk Sultanate

stops.name: Tabriz, the old monk is made an ambassador
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1287; the commissioning seat is given as Maragha in one lens and Tabriz in another, both being Ilkhanid seats in these years, and the pool does not decide between them. The retinue of thirty riding animals is a reconstruction.
stops.campa: The envoy Arghun chooses is a monk of about sixty-seven who has already crossed Asia once on foot. Bar Sauma is a Christian, so the Latin courts must receive him; he is the patriarch's own teacher, so the eastern church stands behind him; and he was born a subject of the Great Khan, so no Ilkhanid faction owns him. He is given letters, gifts, gold, and riding animals, and told to propose a joint campaign against the Mamluks, with Jerusalem handed to the Christians once the two armies have taken it together.
suggested_refs: Arghun's credentials and gifts for the 1287 embassy to the Latin west

stops.name: Trebizond, the Black Sea reached
stops.date_confidence: contested direction: the Yahballaha III itinerary opens with Trabzon, which puts it outbound, while one research lens had made it the return crossing, which nothing supports. Treated here as an outbound landfall. The return port is not recorded anywhere consulted. Month supplied for sequence.
stops.campa: He crosses Armenia overland and comes down to the Black Sea at Trebizond, the Greek port where the Asian roads end and the Genoese ships begin. He has an entourage now, interpreters and clergy and a Genoese agent, and he carries letters from the khan and from the patriarch. The old man who left Khanbaliq to see a tomb is travelling as an ambassador of the house of Hulagu. Nothing in the account suggests he finds this strange. He is about sixty-seven and has been on the road, in one sense or another, for twelve years.
suggested_refs: The Genoese trading colony at Trebizond, gateway between the Ilkhanate and the Black Sea

stops.name: Simisso, taking ship at sixty-seven
stops.date_confidence: attested as the port of embarkation in the Rabban Bar Sauma article; month supplied for sequence. Note that the Yahballaha III itinerary names Trabzon and not Simisso, and the two are not reconciled in the sources.
stops.campa: At Simisso, which the Turks call Samsun, he takes ship. Behind him is every land where a man might reasonably expect to meet another man from Cathay; ahead is a sea, and past it a set of kingdoms his church knows about chiefly from the Acts of the Apostles. He is the first person raised in China of whom we have a written account of this crossing. He does not present himself as such, and the compiler who abridged his book a generation later does not either.
suggested_refs: The Black Sea port of Simisso, modern Samsun

stops.name: Constantinople, before Andronikos II
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1287; no month recorded, supplied for sequence.
stops.campa: Andronikos the Second receives the Mongol khan's ambassador in the city that has been the eastern capital of the world for nine hundred years, and the ambassador, who has prayed all his life in Syriac, walks into Hagia Sophia. He counts the columns, notes the mosaics, describes the dome for readers in Baghdad who will never see it. A monk born in Zhongdu stands under Justinian's roof and takes notes for Persia. The relics of the city are brought out and shown to him one by one.
stops.quote: With the sight of the Christian king fatigue hath vanished and exhaustion hath departed, for I was exceedingly anxious to see your kingdom, the which may our Lord establish!
stops.quote_source: Bar Sauma to Emperor Andronikos II, in E. A. Wallis Budge (tr.), The Monks of Kublai Khan, Emperor of China (1928)
suggested_refs: Hagia Sophia and the relic collections of Palaiologan Constantinople
sources: Budge, The Monks of Kublai Khan (1928)

stops.name: Mount Etna, the mountain burning
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day in his own account; not cross-checked against a volcanological catalogue in this research pass.
stops.campa: Sailing along the Sicilian coast in June, he sees the mountain burning. Fire goes up out of Etna all day and the smoke stands over the sea, and he writes it down: a volcano entered into the record of a monk from Khanbaliq, in Syriac, for an audience in Mesopotamia. The day is the eighteenth of June, and he gives the date exactly, as he gives few other dates on this voyage. He asks what the mountain is, and sets down the answer the local people give him without saying whether he believes it.
suggested_refs: The 1287 eruption of Etna as recorded in the History of Mar Yahballaha and Rabban Sauma

stops.name: The Bay of Naples, the Battle of the Counts
stops.date_confidence: attested to 23 June in the battle historiography; Bar Sauma's own account renders it as 24 June, the feast of Saint John, and two research lenses split on this. Place corrected: the engagement is normally set in the Bay of Naples with the Angevin fleet beached near Castellammare di Stabia, not the Bay of Sorrento. Charles II was an Aragonese prisoner and not in command; the Angevin fleet was led by Reynald Quarrel of Avella under Narjot de Toucy against Roger of Lauria.
stops.campa: Five days later, off the Italian coast, he watches two Christian fleets destroy each other. The Angevins and the Aragonese are fighting the War of the Sicilian Vespers; the Angevin ships are broken and taken, and Bar Sauma sets the dead at twelve thousand. He is carrying to the courts of these same kings a proposal for a joint Christian campaign in Syria. He records what he sees and adds nothing to it. The mission he is carrying to these two courts assumes that Christendom can be moved as one thing.
suggested_refs: The Battle of the Counts, 23 June 1287, and the War of the Sicilian Vespers

stops.name: Rome, a dead pope and a college of cardinals
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1287; the account gives no dates for the Roman audiences, and the four Rome stops in this segment follow the order of the text, not a dated sequence.
stops.campa: He reaches Rome and finds the throne empty: Honorius the Fourth is dead and no successor chosen. The ambassador of the Ilkhan of Persia, sent to treat with the Pope of the Latins, is received instead by cardinals in an interregnum who cannot bind anyone to anything. They ask him who he is. They are still asking hours later, because the answer, a monk of the Church of the East born in the country of the Great Khan, fits nothing they know. He visits the shrine of Saint Peter and waits.
stops.quote: We who are ambassadors of King ARGHON and of the Catholicus of the East [have arrived].
stops.quote_source: Bar Sauma's message to the College of Cardinals during the papal vacancy, in Budge, The Monks of Kublai Khan (1928)
suggested_refs: The papal vacancy of 1287-1288 between Honorius IV and Nicholas IV
sources: Budge, The Monks of Kublai Khan (1928)

stops.name: Rome, the churches of Asia named to the cardinals
stops.date_confidence: attested as an exchange, undated in the account; see the note on the preceding stop.
stops.campa: The cardinals want to know how a Christian deacon comes to be the envoy of a Mongol king. He explains the geography of his own church to them: bishops in Turkestan, in China, among the Mongols and the Turks, congregations standing for centuries that no one in this room has ever counted. Rome has been sending friars east for forty years under the impression that it is opening the road. The man in front of them was ordained at the other end of it, and walked here.
stops.quote: Know ye, O our Fathers, that many of our Fathers have gone into the countries of the Mongols, and Turks, and Chinese and have taught them the Gospel, and at the present time there are many Mongols who are Christians.
stops.quote_source: Bar Sauma to the cardinals in Rome, in Budge, The Monks of Kublai Khan (1928)
suggested_refs: The eastern dioceses of the Church of the East as reported to Rome in 1287
sources: Budge, The Monks of Kublai Khan (1928)

stops.name: Rome, the examination on the faith
stops.date_confidence: attested as an exchange, undated in the account.
stops.campa: Then they examine his faith, and the examination is not friendly. They ask what confession he holds, and he answers that the Apostles taught the East and the East has kept what it was given, and that no man has ever come to them from the Pope. On the procession of the Spirit he is speaking a theology Latin councils have condemned, and he knows it. He does not soften it, and he does not ask them to accept it. The cardinals will tell him afterwards that they had only been testing him.
stops.quote: No man hath come to us Orientals from the Pope. The holy Apostles whose names I have mentioned taught us the Gospel, and to what they delivered unto us we have clung to the present day.
stops.quote_source: Bar Sauma to the cardinals when asked his confession of faith, in Budge, The Monks of Kublai Khan (1928)
suggested_refs: The 'Belief of Rabban Sawma' passage in the History of Mar Yahballaha and Rabban Sauma
sources: Budge, The Monks of Kublai Khan (1928)

stops.name: Rome, the dispute on the procession
stops.date_confidence: attested as an exchange, undated in the account.
stops.campa: The dispute turns to the Trinity, and the old man from Khanbaliq argues logic against the cardinals of Rome in a vocabulary he learned from Syriac books. If the three are coequal in nature and power and dominion, he asks, how can one of them be the cause of another? They press; he does not yield; the exchange is set down in his account at length, which suggests he was proud of it. The text says they held him in high esteem for his skill in argument. The doctrinal question does not move an inch.
stops.quote: If they are coequal in Nature (k'yana), and in operation, and in power, and in authority (or dominion), and the Three Persons (kenome) are One, how is it possible for one of Them to be the cause of the Other? ... We cannot find a demonstration resembling this statement of yours.
stops.quote_source: Bar Sauma disputing Trinitarian procession with the cardinals, in Budge, The Monks of Kublai Khan (1928)
suggested_refs: Latin and East Syriac formulations of the procession of the Spirit, compared in 1287
sources: Budge, The Monks of Kublai Khan (1928)

stops.name: Genoa, the winter and the year of days
stops.date_confidence: corrected: Budge places this exchange at the end of the winter Bar Sauma spent in Genoa, that is early 1288, not 1287 as one research lens had it. The interlocutor is not 'John of Tusculum' but the Periodeutes, the Visitor of Mar Papa, arriving from Allemagne, whom Budge's footnote reports Chabot identifying with John of Jerusalem.
stops.campa: He winters in Genoa, a city of banks and ships where the money that moves between Persia and Flanders is counted. There is still no pope. At the end of the winter a papal Visitor arrives from Germany, and Bar Sauma tells him plainly what the delay is costing: a year gone, an embassy in hand, and nothing to carry back to the Mongols. It is the one moment in the account where the ambassador's patience audibly runs out. He is sixty-eight, and a long way from Baghdad.
stops.quote: What shall I say unto thee, O beloved and noble man? I have come on an embassy from King ARGHON, and the Catholicus of the East to MAR PAPA on the subject of JERUSALEM. Behold I have been a year of days [since I came], and a Pope hath not sat. When I go back what shall I say and what answer can I make to the Moncots?
stops.quote_source: Bar Sauma to the Periodeutes of Mar Papa at Genoa, in Budge, The Monks of Kublai Khan (1928), pp. 187-188
suggested_refs: Genoa as banking and shipping hub between the Ilkhanate and Latin Europe
sources: Budge, The Monks of Kublai Khan (1928)

stops.name: Paris, before Philip the Fair
stops.date_confidence: year unresolved: one lens dates the Paris audience to 1287, another to winter 1287-1288, and the Wikipedia ordering places Paris after the Genoa winter, implying early 1288. Nothing consulted fixes it. Dated 1288 here with the conflict recorded rather than silently resolved.
stops.campa: Philip the Fourth receives him in Paris and stands up to do it. The king asks the two questions a king asks: why have you come, and who sent you. The answer is that Arghun, khan of Persia, and the Catholicus of the East have sent him about Jerusalem. What follows is a month as a guest of the French crown, thirty days of a Mongol ambassador being shown a Latin capital, its scholars, its treasuries, and the relics of the Passion its kings have bought at enormous cost.
stops.quote: And the king stood up before him and paid him honour, and said unto him, "Why hast thou come? And who sent thee?" And RABBAN SAWMA said unto him, "King ARGHON and the Catholicus of the East have sent me concerning the matter of JERUSALEM."
stops.quote_source: The audience with Philip IV at Paris, in Budge, The Monks of Kublai Khan (1928)
suggested_refs: The Passion relics of the French royal chapel, shown to Bar Sauma; the Syriac does not name the building
sources: Budge, The Monks of Kublai Khan (1928)

stops.name: Paris, the promise and the knight
stops.date_confidence: attested: Gobert de Helleville departs on his own mission on 2 February 1288. Philip's reply is undated in the account and is placed with the departure.
stops.campa: Philip's answer is everything the mission was sent for. If the Mongols, who are not Christians, mean to fight the Arabs for Jerusalem, then Christians must certainly fight, and France will go out in strength. He appoints a knight, Gobert de Helleville, to ride east with the embassy, and Helleville sets out on the second of February. Nineteen years later this same king will arrest Jacques de Molay and destroy the Order of the Temple, which by then will have staked its survival on the same Mongol alliance.
stops.quote: If it be indeed so that the Moncots, though they are not Christians, are going to fight against the Arabs for the capture of JERUSALEM, it is meet especially for us that we should fight [with them], and if our Lord willeth, go forth in full strength.
stops.quote_source: Philip IV's reply to Bar Sauma at Paris, in Budge, The Monks of Kublai Khan (1928)
suggested_refs: Gobert de Helleville's mission east, February 1288
sources: Budge, The Monks of Kublai Khan (1928)

stops.name: Bordeaux, the King of England takes communion
stops.date_confidence: the year is unresolved between 1287 and 1288 across the sources, and the day is supplied for sequence only. The place is a conjecture of the editors: Budge prints 'Kasonia (Gascony?)' and 'their city [BORDEAUX?]', so Bordeaux is not stated in the source.
stops.campa: He crosses to Gascony, where Edward the First of England is holding his French lands. Edward hears the proposal and answers that the kings of these countries carry the Cross on their bodies and think of nothing else, and that his mind is easier for knowing the Mongol king thinks as he does. Then he asks the ambassador to celebrate the Eucharist in the rite of the Church of the East, and the King of England receives communion from a monk born at the far end of Asia. He commits no soldiers.
stops.quote: We the kings of these cities bear upon our bodies the sign of the Cross, and we have no subject of thought except this matter. And my mind is relieved on the subject about which I have been thinking, when I hear that King Arghon thinketh as I think.
stops.quote_source: Edward I to Bar Sauma in Gascony, in Budge, The Monks of Kublai Khan (1928), p. 186
suggested_refs: Edward I's Gascon administration in 1287-1288 and his unfulfilled crusade vow
sources: Budge, The Monks of Kublai Khan (1928)

stops.name: Genoa, the loop closed
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction: the return through Genoa is in the itinerary of the Yahballaha III article but is undated.
stops.campa: He recrosses to Genoa on the road back to Rome, closing the loop of the western journey through the same port where he waited out the winter. He has two royal promises and no army. In eleven years the merchants of this city will imprison a Venetian named Marco Polo, who will pass the time dictating an account of Cathay to a fellow prisoner. The two books, his and Polo's, will describe one world from its two ends, and neither man will ever hear of the other.
suggested_refs: The Genoese quarter that housed both Bar Sauma's winter and, eleven years later, Marco Polo's imprisonment

segments.name: The Pope and the Road Home

stops.name: Rome, the Palm Sunday communion
stops.date_confidence: attested to Palm Sunday 1288; the account gives the feast, not the date. Julian Easter 1288 falls on 28 March, which puts Palm Sunday on 21 March.
stops.campa: A pope has been elected at last: Nicholas the Fourth, a Franciscan, the first of his order to hold the see. He receives the ambassador formally, hears the letters of Arghun and of Yahballaha read out, and on Palm Sunday gives Bar Sauma communion with his own hand before the assembled Roman clergy. The monk from the Fangshan hills, examined for heresy by these same cardinals the year before, kneels in Saint Peter's and takes the sacrament from the Bishop of Rome. His account treats this as the height of the journey.
suggested_refs: The election of Nicholas IV, February 1288, and his eastern missionary policy
sources: Budge, The Monks of Kublai Khan (1928)

stops.name: Rome, asking leave to go
stops.date_confidence: attested as an exchange, undated in the account; month supplied for sequence.
stops.campa: He asks leave to go. The Pope has asked him to stay in Rome for good, promising to guard him like the pupil of his eye, and Bar Sauma answers that he came on an embassy and not by his own wish, and that were the wish his own he would end his life at the door of this palace. Then he asks for relics to carry home. Ramon Llull will be in this city within a few years pressing the same pope to send missions to the Tatar khans, and the road east is about to be opened from the Latin end.
stops.quote: O our Father, I came on an embassy for your service. If my coming had been the result of my personal wish, I would willingly bring to an end the days of this my useless life in your service at the outer door of your palace. [But I must return]... Now I beseech your Holiness to bestow upon me some of the relics [of the saints] which ye have with you.
stops.quote_source: Bar Sauma asking leave of Pope Nicholas IV, in Budge, The Monks of Kublai Khan (1928), p. 195
suggested_refs: Nicholas IV's missions east, including John of Montecorvino's journey to Khanbaliq
sources: Budge, The Monks of Kublai Khan (1928)

stops.name: Rome, a few relics for a far country
stops.date_confidence: attested as an exchange, undated in the account. The claim that these relics went into a church at Maragheh is not in the passage and is unsupported.
stops.campa: Nicholas answers that if relics were handed to everyone who asked, mountains of them would have run out long ago, but that a man come from a far country may have a few. Bar Sauma is given a piece of the apparel of Christ, a piece of the kerchief of the Virgin, and fragments of the bodies of saints, with a tiara for the patriarch and letters for the khan. Four centuries later Athanasius Kircher will print the Nestorian Stele of Xi'an and astonish Europe with the news that the Cross had reached China.
stops.quote: If we had been in the habit of giving away these relics to the people [who come] in myriads, even though the relics were as large as the mountains, they would have come to an end long ago. But since thou hast come from a far country, we will give thee a few.
stops.quote_source: Pope Nicholas IV to Bar Sauma, in Budge, The Monks of Kublai Khan (1928), p. 195
suggested_refs: The relics and papal tiara sent from Rome to Patriarch Yahballaha III in 1288
sources: Budge, The Monks of Kublai Khan (1928)

stops.name: Tabriz, the letters laid before Arghun
stops.date_confidence: attested to the summer of 1288 for the return; the month is supplied and the court's location that season is not fixed in the pool.
stops.campa: He comes back to the Ilkhanid court with letters from the King of France, the King of England, and the Pope of Rome, and with the relics, and Arghun is pleased. Proof has been produced that the west can be spoken to. Nothing has been produced that can be spoken to it with: no dates, no numbers, no fleet, no commitment that binds anyone past the season in which it was made. The khan reads the letters as promises. They were written, in every chancery that sealed them, as courtesies.
suggested_refs: The gifts and letters of Philip IV, Edward I, and Nicholas IV delivered to Arghun in 1288

stops.name: Baghdad, home to the patriarch
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1288; month supplied for sequence.
stops.campa: He returns to Baghdad and to the patriarch he made, an old man in the household of a former disciple who now governs the Church of the East from the Ilkhan's own capital region. He has been away two years and has crossed Europe. Nobody in Baghdad can check a word of what he reports, and nobody has reason to doubt it. He begins, in Persian, to write it down: the first description of the Latin west by a man raised in China, composed for readers who will never go there.
suggested_refs: The patriarchal household of Yahballaha III and Bar Sauma's office as visitor-general

stops.name: Tabriz, the letter of the eleventh of May
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day. Place uncertain: the letter's own colophon says it was written at Ho'ndlon, not at the Tabriz chancery, and the pin is the court's seat rather than the scribal place. The popular English rendering of this letter circulates with a scholarly attribution that does not hold, so no quotation from it is used here.
stops.campa: Arghun's chancery drafts a letter to Philip the Fourth on the eleventh of May, in Mongolian, in Uyghur script: if the French warriors come as promised and Egypt falls, Jerusalem is theirs. The khan names the end of the Tiger year's winter as his own date. The letter travels west with Buscarello de Ghizolfi, a Genoese in Mongol service, on a separate embassy, and survives in the archives of France to this day. The campaign it proposes never takes place.
suggested_refs: Arghun's Mongolian letter of 11 May 1289 to Philip IV, Archives Nationales de France

stops.name: Baghdad, the church he builds
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction, and the sources disagree on the place: one has him building a church at Baghdad for the patriarch, another sends the papal relics into a church at Maragheh, which the passage cited for it does not say. Date supplied.
stops.campa: He builds a church, and the sources cannot agree where. One tradition puts it in Baghdad, beside the patriarch he served; another puts it at Maragheh and sends the papal relics into it, which the passage cited for that claim does not say. What is agreed is that the old man spends what he brought back on a building, and that the relics Rome gave to a stranger from a far country end up somewhere in the Ilkhanate, in a church of the communion Rome had spent the previous year examining for heresy.
suggested_refs: The church attributed to Bar Sauma, sited at Baghdad or at Maragheh depending on the source

stops.name: Baghdad, the account written down
stops.date_confidence: attested that he composed the account, undated. The Persian original is lost; the surviving Syriac abridgment is normally placed shortly after Yahballaha III's death in 1317, not 1330 as one research lens had it.
stops.campa: The book takes shape in Persian: the road out of Khanbaliq, Kashgar standing empty, the burning mountain, the fleets breaking in the bay, the cardinals, the two kings, the Pope's hand at the communion. It is the first detailed account of Latin Europe by a man raised in China. It will not survive. What survives is an abridgment in Syriac, made by an anonymous hand a generation later, which cuts his travels down to fit inside a biography of his disciple.
suggested_refs: The lost Persian original and the anonymous Syriac abridgment of the History

stops.name: Acre, the last foothold falls
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day; coordinates inherited from the canonical Acre pin in molay.journey.json. Bar Sauma is not present; the stop marks the fate of the alliance he was sent to arrange.
stops.campa: Acre falls to the Mamluk sultan in May and the last capital of the Latin Kingdom is taken street by street. The joint campaign Bar Sauma spent two years proposing was to have relieved exactly this. Jacques de Molay, who gets away by sea from the Templar house on the shore, will spend the rest of his life pressing the courts of Europe for the alliance with the Ilkhans that the old monk had already been promised twice, in Paris and in Gascony, and given nothing.
suggested_refs: The siege of Acre, May 1291, and the end of the Latin Kingdom

stops.name: Baghdad, death in January
stops.date_confidence: attested to January 1294; no source consulted gives the day, defaulted to 01.
stops.campa: Bar Sauma dies at Baghdad in January, about seventy-three or seventy-four years old, in the service of the patriarch he had raised from a boy in a mountain cell. He had set out to reach Jerusalem and had instead seen Rome, Paris, Gascony, Constantinople, a burning mountain and a sea battle, and had come home to a church about to lose its Mongol protectors. In the same year, at the other end of the world, Kublai Khan dies in the city where Bar Sauma was born.
suggested_refs: The office of visitor-general of the Church of the East, held by Bar Sauma at his death

stops.name: Baghdad, north of the altar
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction, and weakly sourced: the Darath Rhomaye burial comes through a single AI-compiled tertiary source and was not cross-checked against the Montgomery or Budge text in this research pass.
stops.campa: A later retelling puts his body inside the church of Darath Rhomaye, the Convent of the Romans, at Baghdad, laid north of the altar. The detail comes through one compiled source and has not been checked against the Syriac. No tomb, no marker, no identified site has been found. The churches of Baghdad were destroyed and rebuilt and destroyed again in the centuries after the Ilkhanate, and the man received by two kings and a pope has no grave that anyone can visit.
suggested_refs: Darath Rhomaye, the Convent of the Romans at Baghdad, location unidentified
sources: Grokipedia, 'Rabban Bar Sauma' (AI-compiled tertiary source, flagged)

stops.name: Genoa, the other traveller dictates his book
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1298 for Polo's dictation in Genoese captivity; coordinates inherited from the canonical prison pin in marco_polo.journey.json. Included as epilogue, not as a Bar Sauma stop.
stops.campa: In Genoa, four years after Bar Sauma's death, a Venetian prisoner of war dictates to a cellmate a description of Cathay: the Great Khan's cities, the paper money, the Nestorian churches at Kashgar and Ganzhou. Marco Polo's book will be copied into every language of Europe. Bar Sauma's, written first and describing the journey in the other direction, will survive in one abridged Syriac recension that almost nobody reads until 1927. The two men were in this city eleven years apart.
suggested_refs: Rustichello da Pisa's redaction of Marco Polo's Travels, Genoa 1298

stops.name: Maragheh, the disciple dies
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day and place. Corrected: 1294 to 1317 is twenty-three years, over two decades, not the 'nearly three decades' given in one research lens.
stops.campa: Yahballaha the Third outlives his teacher by twenty-three years and dies at Maragheh on the thirteenth of November, having governed the Church of the East for thirty-six years and watched the Ilkhanate turn Muslim around him. He had been consecrated bishop of a Chinese diocese he never reached, and patriarch of a communion he had joined by walking to it. The two monks who left Khanbaliq to see Jerusalem lie buried, one in Baghdad and one in Azerbaijan, and neither of them ever got there.
suggested_refs: The tomb of Yahballaha III at Maragheh and the decline of the Church of the East under the Muslim Ilkhans
